meaning: The Supply section is about how much bitcoin exists and how the amount grows
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Supply

meaning: New bitcoin is created on a schedule that halves the subsidy every 210000 blocks, so the total supply stays just below 21 million.

meaning: The block subsidy halves every 210000 blocks; at block 840000, on 2024-04-20, it fell to 3.125 bitcoin.

meaning: The block subsidy is the amount of new bitcoin that a block may create for its miner; it starts at 50 bitcoin and halves every 210000 blocks.

meaning: The Price section addresses a question that every newcomer asks, namely who sets the price of bitcoin
slide visual: code; drawn shapes; native chart; picture; table
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Price

meaning: The price of bitcoin is set by markets: a floating exchange rate that moves with supply and demand.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A volume-weighted average prices a currency pair by weighting each trade's price by its volume, so larger trades count for more.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The Issuance section is about who creates money and by what rule
slide visual: code; drawn shapes; native chart; table
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Issuance

meaning: A central bank is the institution that controls the creation of a national currency; Bitcoin has none, and its issuance is set by rules.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A clearing house is a central party that records and settles transactions; traditional digital money relied on one, and the term clearing means the confirmation of a payment.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank and replaces the need for any central bank.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Because issuance diminishes and ends, the currency is deflationary over the long term; the last non-zero subsidy falls in the year 2140 at the target pace.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The Network branch is about the community of computers that runs Bitcoin and the way it agrees on a single history without a leader
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Consensus is the state in which the participants of the network agree on the same record of transactions
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Consensus

meaning: Proof of work makes adding a block costly and easy to check; a toy version searches for a number whose SHA-256 hash starts with zeros.
slide visual: code; drawn shapes; native chart; picture; table
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; chapter visual ProofOfWork; lab example

meaning: The double-spend problem is the possibility of spending one unit of digital money twice; Bitcoin's consensus prevents it without a central clearinghouse.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Mining is the repeated computation, referring to a list of recent transactions, by which a participant tries to add a block and earn the reward.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The difficulty of the work is adjusted every 2016 blocks so that, on average, one block is found every 10 minutes whatever the total computing power.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The Byzantine Generals' Problem asks how participants without a leader can agree on a course of action over an unreliable network; Bitcoin's proof of work is a practical solution.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The History section tells where Bitcoin came from
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel History

meaning: The 2008 paper by Satoshi Nakamoto that first described Bitcoin as a purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The software that Nakamoto published in 2009 and many programmers have revised since; Bitcoin Core is its descendant and includes a wallet.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Satoshi Nakamoto is the alias of the person or people who designed Bitcoin; their identity is unknown and they withdrew from the public in April 2011.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Hashcash is a proof-of-work scheme proposed by Adam Back in 1997 to throttle abuse of un-metered resources such as email; Bitcoin's proof of work descends from it.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Digital currencies before Bitcoin used cryptography but were centralized and therefore easy to attack, which is the problem Bitcoin was designed to avoid.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The Standards section collects the two social mechanisms through which Bitcoin is documented and developed: the numbered improvement proposals through which changes are discussed, and the open source licence under which the software is shared
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Standards

meaning: A Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP) is a numbered design document that specifies a change or a convention; BIP 39 describes the mnemonic code behind recovery codes.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Open source software is distributed with its source code under terms that allow free redistribution, modification and derived works.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) is an international organization that develops web standards; its finished standards are called Recommendations.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A wallet is the software through which a person uses Bitcoin
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The platform of a wallet is the kind of device and software environment on which it runs
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel WalletPlatform

meaning: The first type of Bitcoin wallet, run on a general-purpose operating system such as Windows or macOS.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The most common type of Bitcoin wallet, run on a smartphone operating system such as iOS or Android.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A wallet used through a web browser, whose data usually lives on a server owned by a third party.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A hardware signing device stores keys and signs transactions with special-purpose hardware; it must be paired with a full-featured wallet to send and receive.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The node type of a wallet describes how much of the network's work the wallet does for itself
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel NodeType

meaning: A program that validates the entire history of Bitcoin transactions itself and may serve data to other programs.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A client that keeps the wallet locally but relies on a full node or server for most data and validates only partly.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A third-party API client uses a remote system's programming interface instead of the Bitcoin network and trusts it for correct information and privacy.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: In the peer-to-peer network, full nodes are the peers and lightweight wallets are clients that depend on one or more peers for valid data.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Key control is the question of who holds the private keys that unlock a wallet's funds
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel KeyControl

meaning: A wallet where only the user holds the keys, so only the user controls and can lose the bitcoin.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A custodial wallet or account is one where a third party, the custodian, holds the keys and manages the funds for the user.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The Backup section is about getting a wallet back after something goes wrong
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Backup

meaning: A recovery code of words, numbers or letters chosen at random by the wallet, from which all its keys are generated and from which the wallet can be restored.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; chapter visual RecoveryCode; lab example

meaning: Wallet metadata is the data a user adds to a wallet, such as labels on addresses and transactions; a recovery code does not restore it.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The Usage branch follows the chapter's story of Alice and Joe: how Alice receives her first address, how she acquires her first bitcoin, and how Joe sends it
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The Address section explains the destination of a payment
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Address

meaning: A number derived from the private key that others use to pay you; it is registered nowhere, and a new one per invoice protects privacy.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; chapter visual BitcoinAddress

meaning: An invoice is a payment request that a wallet can read, carrying a destination address and often an amount and a description.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Using the same address for several payments lets others link and total them; a new address for each payment protects privacy.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Privacy in Bitcoin is pseudonymous: payments are public and attached to addresses, not names, until an address is linked to an identity.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The Transfer section explains what happens when Joe sends bitcoin to Alice
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Transfer

meaning: Receiving shows an address or invoice; sending signs a transaction that spends to someone else's address.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A transaction is a signed data structure that expresses a transfer of value; it is broadcast over the network, collected into a block, and made permanent on the blockchain.
slide visual: code; drawn shapes; native chart; picture; table
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A transaction's inputs identify the funds it spends and its outputs assign amounts to new owners; any difference between the totals is the fee.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A transaction fee is the amount a sender adds for the miner who includes the transaction in a block; a higher fee gives faster confirmation.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A confirmation counts the blocks that contain a transaction or follow it; each one makes reversal less likely, and the inclusion in a block is the clearing of the payment.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Bitcoin transactions are irreversible, unlike card payments, bank transfers and other electronic payments, which can be reversed.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: An offchain payment moves value without recording every payment in the public blockchain, which lowers cost and improves privacy but changes what a backup must cover.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A payment channel is a class of techniques that lets users make many Bitcoin transactions without committing all of them to the blockchain; typically only two transactions are recorded.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The Lightning Network connects payment channels so that a payment can be routed through several of them, and any peer can pay any other even without a direct channel.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: An electronic payment is a payment made over an electronic network; credit cards, debit cards, PayPal and bank transfers are reversible, unlike Bitcoin transactions.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The semantic bridge connects the chapter's central idea with the theme of this course, semantic technologies
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel SemanticBridge

meaning: A W3C Decentralized Identifier is an identifier that its controller can prove control over without a central registry, applying the principle of control by keys to identity.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A verifiable credential expresses claims made by an issuer, such as a driver's licence or education certificate, in a form protected by digital signatures that a holder can present to a verifier.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The Acquisition section lists the ways in which a newcomer obtains a first bitcoin, which is the practical problem a reader faces as soon as the wallet is installed
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Acquisition

meaning: The least complicated way to get a first bitcoin: buy directly from someone who has some.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Earning bitcoin means selling a product or service and being paid in it.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A Bitcoin ATM is a machine that accepts cash and sends bitcoin to a smartphone wallet.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A currency exchange is a market where buyers and sellers swap bitcoin and local currency, usually through a linked bank account.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Identity verification is the check of a customer's identity and credit-worthiness that companies converting traditional payments into bitcoin usually require.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Cryptography is the science of transforming data so that its meaning is hidden, so that undetected alteration is prevented, or so that unauthorised use is prevented
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Cryptography

meaning: A hash function maps data of any length to a fixed-length fingerprint; SHA-256 produces 256 bits, and any change to the input gives a different result.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A digital signature is a value computed from data and a private key that anyone holding the matching public key can use to verify the origin and integrity of the data.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Public-key cryptography uses a pair of mathematically related keys, one public and one private, so that what one key does only the other can undo.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A private key is the secret half of a key pair; in Bitcoin it is a very large number whose holder alone can sign transactions that spend the corresponding bitcoin.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Entropy is a measure of unpredictability, counted in bits; a wallet needs enough of it that nobody can guess the key or recovery code.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A checksum is a short value computed from data and stored with it so that changes can be detected; a BIP 39 recovery code carries ENT/32 bits taken from a SHA-256 hash.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A keyed hash, or message authentication code, mixes a secret key into a hash so that only a holder of the key can produce or confirm the result; HMAC is the standard construction.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Key stretching derives a key from a secret by repeating a function many times, so that every guess of an attacker costs as much work as the honest computation.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The Chain section explains the data structure at the centre of Bitcoin and the computers that maintain it
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Chain

meaning: A block is a group of transactions, marked with a time and committing to the previous block, that is added to the blockchain once it carries a valid proof of work.
slide visual: code; drawn shapes; native chart; picture; table
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The blockchain is the list of validated blocks, each linking to its predecessor all the way back to the first block; changing an old block breaks every later link.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A timestamp is a recorded time attached to data; each block carries one, and together they place the transactions in an agreed order.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A node is a computer that takes part in the Bitcoin network and runs software that speaks its protocol; full nodes validate blocks and may also route, mine or serve wallets.

meaning: The Computing section explains the ordinary technology on which Bitcoin software runs and by which people reach it
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Computing

meaning: The Internet is a worldwide network of networks that uses the Internet protocol suite; Bitcoin users communicate over it primarily, although other transport networks can be used.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A protocol is a set of rules, formats and procedures that computers follow to exchange data; the Bitcoin protocol is the rules that nodes follow to talk to each other.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: HTTP, the HyperText Transfer Protocol, is the network protocol by which browsers and servers exchange web pages; its requests are plain text.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A web browser is a program that retrieves and displays pages from the web and lets users reach further pages through links.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A server is software or hardware that offers a service to clients over a network; Bitcoin's peer-to-peer design has no central server.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: An API is a set of features and rules by which software interacts with other software; a third-party API client uses a remote system's API instead of the Bitcoin network.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A URI, a Uniform Resource Identifier, is a string that refers to a resource; the bitcoin: scheme of BIP 21 writes an address, an amount and a label as a URI.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A QR code is a two-dimensional matrix barcode that a camera can read; wallets use it to hand over addresses and payment requests without typing.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A database is a storage system that collects organized data so that it is easier to search, structure and extend; a wallet keeps its labels and history in one.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: An operating system is system software that manages a computer's hardware and software resources and provides common services to programs; wallets run on top of one.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A distributed system is a set of computers that communicate over a network and work together; Bitcoin is a distributed system with no central server.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A bit is a binary digit, a byte is eight bits, and a hexadecimal digit stands for four bits; a 256-bit hash is 32 bytes or 64 hexadecimal digits.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The Threats section explains two attacks that chapter 1 warns about by name or by description: malicious software that steals or destroys, and phishing, which tricks a person into handing over a secret
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Threats

meaning: Malware is software intentionally designed to cause harm, to leak information or to gain unauthorised access; fake wallet applications are the chapter's example.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Phishing is a scam in which attackers deceive people into revealing sensitive information or installing malware; a wallet that asks for the recovery code at an unexpected time is a warning sign.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The Nature branch answers a question that precedes all the others: what kind of thing is Bitcoin? Chapter 1 gives two complementary answers
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The Characteristic section collects four properties that the chapter attributes to the bitcoin currency: it is virtual, it is borderless, it is decentralized, and it is robust
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Characteristic

meaning: The bitcoin currency is entirely virtual: there are no physical coins or even individual digital coins, only transactions that imply the coins.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Bitcoin is fast, secure and borderless, which the chapter gives as the reason that it is arguably the perfect form of money for the internet.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Bitcoin is decentralized by design and free of any central authority or point of control that can be attacked or corrupted.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: A robust digital currency is built to withstand intervention by antagonists, whether legitimate governments or criminal elements, which a decentralized design makes possible.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The Architecture section describes how the Bitcoin system is put together
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Architecture

meaning: The Bitcoin protocol defines a decentralized peer-to-peer network in which every full node is a peer that both provides and consumes services.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The second part of Bitcoin is a public transaction journal, the blockchain, in which every confirmed transaction is recorded for anyone to read.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The consensus rules are the set of rules for independent transaction validation and currency issuance that every participant applies in the same way.
